Mightest
MITE-est
v. (2nd pers. sing., aux.)
The second-person singular past of may, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it among the forms of may used with thou. In Scripture it almost always introduces a purpose clause: God did this that thou mightest do or know that.

Biblical Definition

Mightest is a purpose word, and the purposes it introduces are among the plainest statements in Scripture of why God does what He does. At Sinai’s aftermath Moses tells Israel the reason for the whole terrifying display: Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him (Deuteronomy 4:35). The revelation was not given to produce awe as an end in itself but knowledge of the one God, and the monotheism of Israel is grounded on demonstration rather than speculation. Luke opens his Gospel with the same construction: That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed (Luke 1:4) — the aim of an orderly written account is certainty, which is a striking claim for a book so often read as though certainty were beyond it. Ananias states the purpose of his errand to a blind persecutor: hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost (Acts 9:17). And Paul charges Timothy with the purpose of the prophecies spoken over him: that thou by them mightest war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) — gifts and prophecies given not for the man’s comfort but for his campaign.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives MIGHTEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the auxiliary verb MAY, used with thou: expressing possibility, liberty, or purpose — that thou mightest know, that is, in order that thou shouldest be able to know.

expand to see more

MIGHTEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the auxiliary verb MAY; used with the pronoun thou.

MAY, aux. v. — To be possible; to express liberty, permission, or opportunity.

In the past tense, used to express the end or purpose of an action; as, this was done that thou mightest know.

Also expressing wish or desire; as, might it be so; and in Scripture, the design of God in a providence.

From Saxon magan, to be able — the root also of might, main, and dismay.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 4:35 — "Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him."

Luke 1:4 — "That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed."

Acts 9:17 — "And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost."

1 Timothy 1:18 — "This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare;"

Modern Corruption

Luke 1:4 says the Gospel was written so that its reader might know the certainty of what he had been taught, and the modern instinct that treats certainty about Christian claims as arrogance sets that stated purpose aside.

expand to see more

Luke is explicit about method and aim. He had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, he consulted eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word, he wrote in order, and he did it so that Theophilus mightest know the certainty. That is a historian’s claim and it invites examination. Against it stands the now-common assumption that religious knowledge is a different species of knowledge, warm but unverifiable, and that anyone claiming certainty about the resurrection has confused faith with evidence. The New Testament does not agree. Paul names witnesses and challenges his readers to go and ask them; Peter denies that the apostles followed cunningly devised fables; John writes so that his readers may know that ye have eternal life. Certainty is the stated goal, and humility about oneself is not the same thing as agnosticism about Christ.

Deuteronomy 4:35 guards the same ground from the other side. The plagues, the sea, the mountain and the voice were shown to Israel for a stated reason: that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him. Modern religious pluralism reverses this, treating the exclusive claim as the offensive part and the experience as the acceptable residue. But the exclusivity is the point of the demonstration; a God who is one among several would not need the Red Sea to establish it. 1 Timothy 1:18 adds the practical note that keeps knowledge from turning into mere possession: the prophecies were given Timothy so that he might fight with them. Doctrine held and not used for war is doctrine half received.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hina (G2443), in order that — the purpose conjunction the KJV renders with that…mightest; dunamai (G1410), to be able; Hebrew lemaan (H4616), to the intent that, for the sake of.

expand to see more

Greek hina (G2443) — in order that; the purpose particle behind most New Testament that thou mightest clauses.

Greek hopos (G3704) — so that, to the end that; the near synonym of hina in purpose constructions.

Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the root of dunamis, power, and the English dynamic.

Hebrew lemaan (H4616) — to the intent that, for the sake of; that thou mightest know in Deuteronomy 4:35.

Greek asphaleia (G803) — certainty, safety, that which cannot be made to slip; Luke’s stated aim in Luke 1:4.

Usage

"That thou mightest know that the LORD he is God (Deuteronomy 4:35) — the purpose of the whole exodus display."

"That thou mightest know the certainty (Luke 1:4) — a historian’s stated aim in writing a Gospel."

"That thou by them mightest war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) — gifts given for a campaign, not for comfort."
